A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same interchangeable-token embedding work. Their complete main texts, appendices, equations, tables, and figures support reliable comparison, including matching material moved into v2's appendices.

before.justification: v1 reports original Transformer experiments on copying and LTL solving, including edit distances, correctness rates, alpha-covariance, and sensitivity to embedding randomness.

after.justification: v2 retains original experiments and adds alpha-renaming baseline evaluations and larger-vocabulary alpha-covariance results, with additional results in Appendices A.3–A.4.

M1.justification: The proposed dual-part embeddings, random-vector generators, normalization, three-way weight tying, and adapted AdaCos loss remain unchanged. Alpha-renaming augmentation is introduced as a comparison method, not a modification of the proposed method.

E1.justification: Both versions cover the same synthetic copying tasks and vocabulary/length ranges, LTLRandom35, its perturbed and limited-data variants, and LTL generalization to 10 APs and length 50. New comparisons and alpha-covariance measurements use this existing coverage.

E2.justification: v2 adds an evaluated alpha-renaming augmentation baseline alongside the original and full-vocabulary fixed-embedding baselines. It participates in copying, LTL perturbation, limited-data, and generalization comparisons, providing a substantial alternative explanation for the proposed method's benefits.

E3.justification: v2 adds a larger-vocabulary alpha-covariance protocol using 1,000 examples with 120 random alpha-equivalent variants each, alongside the retained exhaustive five-AP evaluation. It also reports LTL RoPE/AdaCos validation controls. Section 5.2.3 changes the stated configuration from dα=5 to dβ=5 without establishing that the experiment was rerun.

E4.justification: New Table 3 tests alpha-conversion robustness in the vocabulary-generalization regime, substantially extending evidence about whether invariance survives expansion. v2 also extends perturbation, limited-data, and normalization analyses to the alpha-renaming baseline and reports LTL RoPE/AdaCos controls. The existing embedding-randomness and 277-model correlation analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions retain best-of-at-least-three training-run reporting, ten embedding randomizations, the same standard-deviation analysis, and correlation p-values. Moving the correlation analysis to Appendix A.3.1 does not change statistical practice. The new copying-variance caveat adds interpretation rather than a new uncertainty estimate.

E6.justification: v2 adds alpha-renaming results, including copying edit distance 1.85 and LTL generalization correctness 85.81%, plus the larger-vocabulary alpha-covariance table. Existing LTL values also change: normal-baseline correctness goes from 97.96% to 98.23%, and limited-data proposed correctness from 87.62% to 87.32% (v1 Table 4; v2 Tables 2 and 7). The original Figure 4 scores, including proposed correctness 92.87%, remain unchanged.

T1.justification: New Section 3 formally defines the vocabulary partition, semantics-preserving token bijections, and post-training vocabulary-extension requirement. No theorem or proof is added. Equation 2's replacement of n with |P| is equivalent under the existing definition; the embedding and LTL syntax equations are retained.

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction now include alpha-renaming augmentation as an explicit alternative, with an originality claim in the introduction. The central generalization and inductive-bias claims remain. Alpha-covariance is newly foregrounded in the abstract but was already a claimed contribution in v1.

C2.justification: v2 adds hypotheses about shared semantic embeddings and avoidance of token-specific biases to explain advantages over alpha-renaming. It questions the significance of copying differences because of training variance, elaborates the in-distribution/generalization tradeoff, and identifies meaningful variable names as an unexplored applicability issue.

D1.justification: v2 newly specifies retained LTL evaluation sample counts, embedding selection and reuse during alpha-covariance evaluation, and constant epochs with approximately tenfold fewer steps for limited-data training. It also documents baseline augmentation, reproduction from scratch, and computing facilities. The main hyperparameter table is relocated with its numerical values retained.

R1.justification: The cited works are unchanged. v2 adds positioning through its claimed novel internal alpha-renaming baseline, an explicit assertion that no existing metric measures the targeted robustness, and discussion of reproducing Hahn et al. (2021).

P1.justification: v2 reorganizes the narrative around a new Problem Definition, moves language-model preliminaries, hyperparameter analysis, and limited-data discussion into appendices, and centralizes baseline descriptions. It also edits the abstract and introduction, expands experimental discussion, and adds acknowledgments.

P2.justification: The opening copying visualization moves into Section 5.1. Figure 3 replaces the full-length copying panel with an alpha-renaming panel, while retaining the former result in text. Figure 4 changes from three panels to a four-panel grid. Tables are relocated, split, and expanded, including new Table 3 and the combined appendix comparison in Table 7.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses a central evidential gap in v1 by testing whether simple alpha-renaming augmentation can provide the same benefits. The added baseline matches scaled-up copying performance and exceeds the proposed method on reported five-AP LTL tests, but trails in LTL generalization (85.81% versus 92.87% in Figure 4). This makes the comparison substantially more informative and exposes meaningful tradeoffs. Formal task definitions and clearer evaluation details further strengthen the paper, although best-run selection and limited uncertainty reporting remain.
